case_name: Colter Developments Ltd. v. Squamish JV Ltd.
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Colter Developments Ltd. v.

Squamish JV Ltd.,

2015 BCSC 415

Date: 20150317

Docket:
S113034

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Colter
Developments Ltd. dba Colter Developments, Granite Art Masonry Ltd., Pipeline
Mechanical Inc., Fisher Painting Ltd., 635913 B.C. Ltd. dba Mustang Contracting
Corp., and C & E Building Products Inc.

Plaintiffs

And

Squamish
JV Ltd., Venture West Hotels Group Ltd., Brian John Keith Ostrander, Michael
David Babcock, Jr., also known as Michael Babcock, Hospitality West Management
Group Ltd., High River JV Ltd., "Camrose", Servus Credit Union Ltd.

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Pearlman

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiffs:

G.
Kim

Counsel for the Defendant, Babcock:

David
E.C. Turner

Sarah
E. Orr

Counsel for the Defendant, Servus Credit
Union:

Kimberly
A. Robertson

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

February
27, 2015

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

March
17, 2015

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The plaintiffs and the defendant Servus Credit
Union Ltd. ("Servus") bring cross-applications.

[
2
]

By their further amended notice of application
filed February 24, 2015, the plaintiffs apply pursuant to Rule 6-1(1)(b)(i) of
the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
for leave to amend their further amended notice
of civil claim.

[
3
]

For its part, Servus applies under Rule 22-4(2)
for an order extending the time to file a counterclaim.  Servus also seeks an
order pursuant to the inherent jurisdiction of the court and
s.236
of the
Business
Corporations Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, ("
BCA
"), requiring
the plaintiffs to post security for the costs of Servus in the action in the
amount of $47,460.  Servus requests that the action be stayed until the
plaintiffs have posted the security for costs ordered by the court, and that in
the event the plaintiffs fail to post the security ordered within 30 days of
the date of the court's order, the action against Servus be dismissed, without
prejudice to the defendant's counterclaim.

BACKGROUND
FACTS

[
4
]

Counsel for the parties appearing on these
applications have helpfully provided an Agreed Statement of Facts, from which
the following facts are largely drawn.

[
5
]

On or about April 18, 2008, the plaintiff,
Colter Developments Ltd. dba Colter Developments ("Colter"), entered
into a construction management agreement with the defendant Venture West Hotels
Group Ltd. ("VW Hotels") on behalf of Squamish JV Ltd. ("Squamish
JV").  Colter agreed to provide construction management services and other
work and materials for a project known as the Holiday Inn Express - Squamish BC
(the "Holiday Inn project").  Colter remains unpaid for certain work
it undertook on the Holiday Inn project.  The other plaintiffs are all unpaid
trades that worked on the Holiday Inn project.

[
6
]

The defendants VW Hotels and Squamish JV were
the owners and developers of the Holiday Inn project.  Squamish JV was the
registered owner of lands in the District of Squamish on which the Holiday Inn
project was constructed.

[
7
]

The defendant Brian John Keith Ostrander was a
director of Squamish JV and the sole director of VW Hotels, which in turn was a
majority shareholder of Squamish JV.  Mr. Ostrander was also the sole
director and shareholder of the defendant Hospitality West Management Group
Ltd., which held a majority of shares in VW Hotels.  In addition, Mr. Ostrander
was the sole director of the defendant High River JV Ltd.  The plaintiffs
allege that Mr. Ostrander was the directing mind of all of those corporate
defendants.

[
8
]

The defendants Squamish JV, VW Hotels, Hospitality
Management Group Ltd. and High River JV Ltd. have all been dissolved or struck
from the applicable corporate registries.

[
9
]

On November 2, 2012 the Honourable Master Scarth
granted the plaintiffs an order for substitutional service of their amended
notice of civil claim on Mr. Ostrander.  Pursuant to that order, the
plaintiffs served Mr. Ostrander by forwarding a copy of the pleadings and
the entered substituted service order by ordinary mail to Mr. Ostrander's
father's residence in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and by leaving a copy of those
documents at the front door of Mr. Ostrander's father's Saskatoon
residence.

[
10
]

Mr. Ostrander has not filed and served a
response to civil claim in this action.

[
11
]

The only defendants appearing on these
applications are Mr. Michael D. Babcock, Jr. and Servus.

[
12
]

Mr. Babcock was an investor in the Holiday
Inn project and a shareholder in VW Hotels.  The plaintiffs allege that on
October 26, 2009 Mr. Babcock induced them to return to work on the Holiday
Inn project by promising to pay them in his personal capacity.  The plaintiffs
have claimed against Mr. Babcock for negligent misrepresentation, or
alternatively, breach of an oral contract.  By their proposed second further amended
notice of civil claim, the plaintiffs seek to advance an alternative claim in
unjust enrichment against Mr. Babcock.

[
13
]

The defendant Servus was the commercial secured
lender to Squamish JV.  The plaintiffs claim that Servus knowingly assisted
Squamish JV in wrongfully diverting funds that Servus had advanced to Squamish
JV under its loan.  The plaintiffs seek a declaration that the advances made by
Servus were impressed with a trust in favour of the plaintiffs and that the
diversion of funds constituted a breach of trust.

[
14
]

On November 14, 2008, Servus agreed to loan
Squamish JV the principal amount of $8,896,550 (the "mortgage loan"),
for the Holiday Inn project.  Repayment was secured by a mortgage and a general
security agreement in favour of Servus charging collateral that included the
lands on which the Holiday Inn project was located.  Servus perfected all of
its security through registration of the mortgage in the Land Title Office and
its general security instrument in the Personal Property Security Registry.

[
15
]

Between February 4, 2009 and March 10, 2010, the
plaintiff Colter executed Statutory Declarations of Progress Payment
Distribution forms by which Colter declared personal knowledge of the fact
that:

… all accounts for labour, subcontracts, products, services,
and construction machinery and equipment which have been incurred directly by
the Contractor in the performance of work as required by the Contract, and which
the Owner might in any way be held responsible, have been paid in full as
required by the Contract, up to and including the latest progress payment
received as identified above …

Some of the statutory declarations bore
notations of partial payment only.

[
16
]

Between February 18, 2009 and March 12, 2010,
Servus advanced a total of $8,794,127 to Squamish JV.

[
17
]

On various dates between March 24, 2010 and
April 12, 2010, each of the plaintiffs, other than C & E Building Products
Inc., filed builders' liens against the Holiday Inn project property.

[
18
]

On August 10, 2010, after Squamish JV had
breached the mortgage loan, Servus demanded payment in full of the amounts
owing.  Shortly thereafter, Servus brought proceedings to enforce the mortgage
loan and the personal property security in
Servus Credit Union Ltd. v.
Squamish JV Ltd.
, BCSC action number S105562 (the "Servus proceedings").

[
19
]

By order pronounced August 31, 2010 in the
Servus proceedings, Myers Norris Penny Ltd. ("MNP") was appointed as
interim receiver over the assets, undertakings and properties of Squamish JV.
Subsequently, on November 24, 2010, MNP was appointed Receiver Manager under
the
Bankruptcy and

Insolvency

Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3.

[
20
]

On March 14, 2010 by the distribution order made
in the Servus proceedings, on notice to the plaintiffs, Colter, Pipeline
Mechanical Inc., 635913 B.C. Ltd. and C & E Building Products
Inc., the proceeds of sale and liquidation of the assets and undertakings of
Squamish JV by MNP were distributed.  Servus realized $4 million from the sale
of the assets, including the Holiday Inn project lands.  The amount owed to
Servus was approximately $9.4 million, resulting in a shortfall of
approximately $5.4 million.  Neither the plaintiffs nor Mr. Babcock
realized anything from the sale of the Squamish JV assets.

DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS

Plaintiffs' application to file and serve second further amended notice
of civil claim

[
21
]

The principles which govern the granting of
amendments to pleadings, as summarized by McLachlin J., as she then was, in
Victoria
Grey Metro Trust Co. v. Fort Gary Trust Co.,

1982 CanLII 227 (BC SC)
, [1982] B.C.J No. 1500, 30
B.C.L.R. (2d) 45 at para.
2
, include the following:

(a) such amendments should be permitted as
are necessary to determine the real question in issue between the parties;

(b) the rules will be interpreted to permit
the just and speedy determination of the dispute on its merits;

(c) the
Law and Equity Act
, R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 253, s. 10 “requires the court to grant all such remedies as any of
the parties may appear to be entitled to ‘so that, as far as possible, all
matters in controversy between the parties may be completely and finally
determined …’”;

(d) the court will take a generous approach
to the question of amendments;

(e) the court will not allow useless
amendments;

(f) the court
will not give its sanction to amendments which violate the rules which govern
pleadings, including the requirements relating to conciseness, material fact,
particulars and the prohibition against pleadings which disclose no reasonable
claim or are otherwise scandalous, frivolous or vexatious.

[
22
]

In exercising its discretion judicially, the
court will take into account the length of delay, the reasons for delay, the
expiry of any limitation period, the presence or absence of prejudice, and the
extent of any connection between the existing claims and the proposed new cause
of action.  None of these factors should be considered in isolation.  The
overriding question is what is just and convenient:
Teal Cedar Products

(1977)
Ltd. v. Dale Intermediaries Ltd.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 3033 (BC CA)
, 19 B.C.L.R. (3d) 282 at paras.
67
,
74 (C.A.).

[
23
]

Rule 3-1(2) requires the notice of civil claim
to set out a concise statement of the material facts giving rise to the claim.
A proposed amendment is deficient and should not be allowed where it is
unsupported by material facts:
Salico Property Marketing Corp. v. Farris
Vaughan Wills & Murphy
,
2009 BCSC 1489
at para.
72
.

[
24
]

I turn now to the proposed amendments.

[
25
]

The proposed amendment to paragraph 4 of the
statement of facts pleads facts relating to the receivership of the plaintiff
Pipeline Mechanical Inc. (“Pipeline”), and the assignment of Pipeline’s claim
against the defendants to Colter and 635193 B.C. Ltd. dba Mustang Contracting
Corp. (“Mustang”).  The proposed amendment to paragraph 68 pleads that the
plaintiffs’ reliance on the assurances and representations of Mr. Babcock, against
whom the plaintiffs have claimed damages for misrepresentation and breach of
contract since the delivery of their amended notice of civil claim in May
2012.  The proposed amendments to the relief sought at pages 11 and 12 of the
second further amended notice of civil claim plead the plaintiffs’ claims for personal
judgments against Mr. Ostrander and Mr. Babcock, and clarify the relief claimed
jointly and severally against all of the defendants.

[
26
]

In my view, the proposed amendments to
paragraphs 4 and 68 of the statement of facts and to the remedies sought at
pages 10 and 11 plead material facts or assist in determining the real
questions in issue by identifying the relief sought against particular
defendants.  Those amendments are not useless.  Neither Servus nor Mr. Babcock
have suggested that they will be prejudiced by those amendments.  The
plaintiffs are granted leave to make those amendments.

[
27
]

The amendments that Servus and Mr. Babcock
respectively strenuously oppose are the proposed amendment to paragraph 51of
the statement of facts concerning the terms on which Colter compiled and
submitted its statutory declarations regarding amounts owing on the Holiday Inn
project, and the proposed addition of a new claim in unjust enrichment against
Mr. Babcock.

[
28
]

At paragraph 51 of the proposed second further
amended notice of civil claim, the plaintiffs plead:

51.       The
terms of the Credit Facility required the following:

a.         Colter compile and submit
reports of amounts owing to itself
and the Trade Contractors
to Squamish
JV (the
"Payment Reports")
;

b.         Squamish JV forward the
reports to Servus; and

c.         only
upon receiving the Payment Reports, Servus authorize the drawing down of funds
from the Credit Facility, and forward the funds to Squamish JV for the express
purpose of paying Colter and the Trade Contractors (the
"Authorized
Funds")
.

[
29
]

Servus takes the position that the plaintiffs,
without having brought an application to do so, are seeking to withdraw an
admission that Colter submitted the statutory declarations (described in the
pleadings as “Payment Reports”), on its own behalf, and on behalf of the other
trades.

[
30
]

Rule 7-7(5)(c) provides that a party is not
entitled to withdraw an admission made in a pleading except by consent or with
leave of the court.  The type of admission contemplated by Rule 7-7(5)(c) is an
admission which would benefit the opposing party in its prosecution of the case
following the amendment.  The admission must be a deliberate concession made by
one party for the benefit of the opposing party:
Kamei Sushi Japanese
Restaurant Ltd. v. Epstein
(1996),
1996 CanLII 1682 (BC SC)
, 25 B.C.L.R. (3d) 366 (S.C.) at para.
12
.

[
31
]

In my view, the current pleading in paragraph 51
falls short of a deliberate and unambiguous admission that Colter completed and
filed the statutory declarations not only on its own behalf, but on behalf of
the other trades.  Accordingly, the plaintiffs’ proposed amendment to paragraph
51 does not contravene Rule 7-7(5)(c).

[
32
]

Further, the nature and extent of Colter’s
obligations under the terms of the credit facility is a triable issue to be
determined on its merits at trial.  To the extent that issue involves the
interpretation of the terms of the form of statutory declaration sworn by
Colter, that issue is one of mixed fact and law.  Although there has been delay
on the part of the plaintiff in making the amendment to paragraph 51 of the
proposed second further amended notice of civil claim, Servus has not shown
that it has suffered any significant prejudice as a result of that delay.
Servus’ representative has not yet been examined for discovery.  No trial date
has been set.  Any prejudice to Servus in now having to join issue with the
plaintiffs on the meaning of Colter’s statutory declarations is outweighed by
the interests of justice in having that  issue determined on the merits.
Accordingly, I permit the amendment proposed to paragraph 51.

[
33
]

I turn now to the proposed pleading of unjust
enrichment against Mr. Babcock.

[
34
]

The plaintiffs filed their application to
further amend their notice of claim on January 29, 2015; three days after
counsel for Mr. Babcock had filed and served his application for dismissal
of the plaintiffs' claim against him by summary trial.

[
35
]

In support of their notice of application, the
plaintiffs filed affidavit no. 1 of Ms. Beatrice Liu, a legal assistant
employed by the plaintiffs’ solicitors.  Ms. Liu deposed on information
and belief that following Mr. Babcock's examination for discovery of
August 27, 2014, plaintiffs' counsel determined that the further amended
statement of claim required further amendments to properly set out:

(a)       the pleading of unjust enrichment against all the
defendants, including Mr. Babcock; and

(b)       the remedy of personal judgments against Mr. Babcock
and Mr. Ostrander.

[
36
]

By the time this application came on for hearing,
the plaintiffs had amended their notice of application to assert the further
amended statement of claim required amendment to properly set out the unjust
enrichment claim against Mr. Babcock only.

[
37
]

While the plaintiffs have claimed against VW
Hotels and other corporate defendants for unjust enrichment since the
commencement of this action in 2011, they do not assert that cause of action
against Servus, and have not previously raised it against Mr. Babcock.

[
38
]

The plaintiffs have provided no particulars in
their materials of any new information or evidence gleaned from the discovery
of Mr. Babcock that led them to conclude they had a cause of action against him
for unjust enrichment.

[
39
]

In part 3 of the second further amended notice
of civil claim, the plaintiffs plead at para. 16:

16.       In the
alternative, Babcock induced the plaintiffs to suffer further damages and loss
by returning to the job site and completing the construction of the
Improvement.
In his own personal capacity, Babcock made representations and
induced the plaintiffs into completing the Improvement, thereby enhancing and
safeguarding his investment.  As a result of the plaintiffs' reasonable
reliance on Babcock's assurances and representations and the completion of the
Improvement, the defendants Babcock and the shareholders of Squamish JV and VW
Hotels have been enriched, and the plaintiffs correspondingly deprived, and
there is no juristic reason for the enrichment.

[
40
]

Mr. Babcock opposes the amendment on the
following grounds:

(a)       there is no factual basis for the new cause of action
against Mr. Babcock in the proposed pleading;

(b)       the new claim against Mr. Babcock does not disclose a
reasonable claim, and is useless;

(c)        Mr. Babcock is prejudiced by the amendment; and

(d)       the balance of convenience strongly favours dismissal of
the amendment application.

No material facts supporting claim for unjust enrichment against Mr. Babcock

[
41
]

The elements of a claim of unjust enrichment are
enrichment of the defendant, a corresponding deprivation to the plaintiff, and
the absence of any juristic reason for the enrichment:
Garland v. Consumers’
Gas Co.
,
2004 SCC 25
.

[
42
]

The plaintiffs have failed to allege facts
indicating that Mr. Babcock was enriched.  At paragraph 21 of their pleadings,
the plaintiffs allege that Mr. Babcock was at all material times a shareholder
of the VW Hotels.  At paragraph 55, they plead that Squamish JV, VW Hotels, or
Mr. Ostrander wrongfully diverted, or caused to be diverted funds allocated for
the Holiday Inn project, and that $764,341.97 was wrongfully diverted to VW
Hotels.  The plaintiffs have not pleaded that Mr. Babcock personally
received or benefitted from any of those funds.

[
43
]

Neither the defendants nor the court should be
left to guess at the bases for the plaintiffs’ claim against Mr. Babcock.

[
44
]

To the extent that the plaintiffs may be
asserting that Mr. Babcock benefitted through his shareholding in VW Hotels,
that claim is foreclosed by the plaintiffs’ failure to plead any facts that
would support the piercing of the corporate veil.  As Mr. Justice Burnyeat
stated in
Malik (Representative ad litem of) v. State Petroleum Corp.
,
2007
BCSC 739
at para.
29
:

It is a well settled proposition of law that a company has a
separate legal existence independent from that of its shareholders:  Salomon v.
Salomon & Co. Ltd.,
[1897] A.C. 22 (H.L.)
.  By invoking the words “unjust
enrichment”, the limited liability enjoyed by shareholders cannot be
circumvented.  The liability of a shareholder for the actions of the company is
limited to the shares held by the shareholder in the company. …

[
45
]

The plaintiffs have failed to plead material
facts supporting an enrichment of Mr. Babcock, an essential element for any
cause of action for unjust enrichment against that defendant.

Proposed
pleading has no reasonable prospect of success

[
46
]

The bare assertion of the elements of unjust
enrichment, without the pleading of material facts supporting each of those
elements, is an insufficient pleading of the proposed cause of action against
Mr. Babcock.

[
47
]

Not only have the plaintiffs failed to plead
facts supporting an enrichment of Mr. Babcock, they have also failed to clearly
plead material facts supporting a corresponding deprivation.  The pleading at
paragraph 68, that “as a result of relying on the Babcock Agreement and
Babcock’s assurances and representations to the plaintiffs, the plaintiffs
incurred further liability” is not a clear or concise pleading that the
plaintiffs suffered a deprivation corresponding to some enrichment of Mr.
Babcock.

[
48
]

While the plaintiffs have pleaded that Mr.
Babcock was an investor in VW Hotels, they have not alleged any conduct on his
part that would warrant piercing the corporate veil.  There is no allegation
that Mr. Babcock dominated or controlled any of the corporate defendants or
somehow used VW Hotels as a shield for fraudulent and improper conduct:
XY,
LLC v. Zhu
,
2013 BCCA 352
at para.
88
.

[
49
]

I accept the submission of counsel for Mr.
Babcock that the claim against him for unjust enrichment is bound to fail, and
is therefore “useless”.

Evolution of
plaintiffs’ pleadings of unjust enrichment

[
50
]

When the plaintiffs filed their original notice
of civil claim in May 2011, they alleged unjust enrichment against the
corporate defendants.

[
51
]

Almost four years after the commencement of this
action, the plaintiffs first raised their allegation of unjust enrichment
against Mr. Babcock.

[
52
]

On January 26, 2015, Mr. Babcock delivered his
application for the dismissal by summary trial of the plaintiffs’ claims
against him, which were then framed in negligent misrepresentation and breach
of contract.

[
53
]

On January 29, 2015, the plaintiffs filed their
application to amend their pleadings by alleging unjust enrichment against Mr.
Babcock.

[
54
]

In the version of their proposed second further
amended notice of civil claim attached to their notice of application filed on
January 29, 2015, the plaintiffs pleaded that as “a shareholder of VW Hotels”,
Mr. Babcock made the representations and inducements alleged to give rise to
his unjust enrichment.

[
55
]

On February 23, 2015, counsel for Mr. Babcock
filed an amended application response in which they argued that “the proposed
amendment is claiming against a shareholder for the wrongs of the company … The
Plaintiffs are attempting to pierce the corporate veil without any grounds to
do so ….”

[
56
]

On February 24, 2015, the plaintiffs delivered
their further amended notice of application in which they substituted the words
“in his own personal capacity” for “as a shareholder of VW Hotels” at paragraph
16 of their proposed amendment.

[
57
]

The plaintiffs appear to have hastily amended
their proposed pleading of unjust enrichment against Mr. Babcock in an effort
to meet their opponents’ submission that the claim of unjust enrichment against
Mr. Babcock as a shareholder of VW Hotels was a flawed attempt to pierce the
corporate veil.

[
58
]

The plaintiffs have provided no particulars of
any new evidence emerging from the examination for discovery of Mr. Babcock
that would explain their lengthy delay in pleading unjust enrichment against
him.  Rather than answering Mr. Babcock’s application for dismissal of their
claims against him on the current pleadings, the plaintiffs, through their
application to amend their pleadings by adding the claim of unjust enrichment,
and the amendments to that application, have endeavoured, as counsel for Mr.
Babcock put it, “to move the goal posts on Mr. Babcock”.

Prejudice

[
59
]

Mr. Babcock will suffer prejudice if he is now
put to the trouble and expense of defending a claim of unjust enrichment that
is inadequately pleaded, that will increase the complexity of the action as
against him, and that was first raised almost four years after the commencement
of this action.  Answering a claim of unjust enrichment would require
investigations going well beyond those necessary to meet the plaintiffs' claims
of negligent misrepresentation and breach of an oral contract, which arise from
a single meeting between Mr. Babcock and representatives of the plaintiffs on
October 26, 2009.

Conclusion on Plaintiffs’
application to amend pleadings

[
60
]

I have found that the plaintiffs have failed to
plead essential elements for a cause of action of unjust enrichment against Mr.
Babcock; that the proposed claim of unjust enrichment against Mr. Babcock is
bound to fail; that there has been lengthy and unexplained delay on the part of
the plaintiffs; and that Mr. Babcock would be prejudiced by the proposed
amendment.

[
61
]

Over the last three years, the plaintiffs have already
twice amended their notice of civil claim to add or amend claims against Mr.
Babcock.

[
62
]

In all of these circumstances, this is not a
case where the court should afford the plaintiffs another opportunity to recast
their pleadings by dismissing the present application to add the claim of
unjust enrichment against Mr. Babcock with liberty to re-apply.

[
63
]

Accordingly, I deny the plaintiffs leave to
amend their pleadings to claim against Mr. Babcock for unjust enrichment.

[
64
]

In the result, the plaintiffs have leave to make
all of the amendments sought, other than the addition of the claim in unjust
enrichment against Mr. Babcock.

Plaintiffs’ application for substituted service

[
65
]

The plaintiffs also apply for an order that
their further amended notice of civil claim and second further amended notice
of civil claim be served on Mr. Ostrander by the following alternative methods
of service:

(a)       by forwarding a copy of the said documents
by ordinary mail, together with a copy of the entered substituted service
order, to Mr. Ostrander’s father’s residential address at 2312 Preston Avenue,
Saskatoon, Saskatchewan; and

(b)       leaving
a copy of the said documents, together with a copy of the entered substituted
service order, on the front door of Mr. Ostrander’s father’s residential
address of 2312 Preston Avenue, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan.

[
66
]

During the hearing of these applications, I ruled
that I was satisfied that the plaintiffs had made diligent efforts to serve Mr.
Ostrander personally with their further amended notice of civil claim, had made
reasonable efforts to locate Mr. Ostrander, and that personal service was
impracticable.

[
67
]

The order for alternative service sought by the
plaintiffs is on essentially the same terms as the order granted by Master
Scarth in November 2012.

[
68
]

The order for alternative service is granted and
will apply not only to service on Mr. Ostrander of the further amended notice
of civil claim and the second further amended notice of civil claim, but also
to service on Mr. Ostrander of any further process issued by the plaintiffs in
this action.

Application of Servus to file Counterclaim

[
69
]

Servus applies for an order extending the time
to file its counterclaim against Colter for damages for fraudulent or negligent
misrepresentation.

[
70
]

By its proposed counterclaim, Servus pleads that
in keeping with its lending practice, each of the loan advances to Squamish JV
was made only after a construction draw request was made by that defendant,
accompanied by the following documents:

(a)       a progress report completed by a professional quantity
surveyor providing a progress certificate and detailed project cost breakdown
to support the advance requested;

(b)       a borrower's declaration by which Squamish JV represented,
certified and guaranteed that all:

... Contractors, subcontractors, suppliers
of material, suppliers of services and other persons participating in the
construction of the project are in good standing and the Developer is not in
default in payment of any sums to such parties or fulfillment of any of its
obligations with respect thereto.

(c)        a Statutory Declaration of Progress Payment Distribution
by Contractor, by which Colter solemnly declared that it had personal knowledge
of the fact that:

... all accounts for labour, subcontracts,
products, services, and construction machinery and equipment which had been
incurred directly by the Contractor in the performance of the work as required
by the Contract, and for which the owner in any way might be held responsible,
have been paid in full as required by the Contract, up to and including the
latest progress payment received….

[
71
]

Servus alleges that Colter's statutory
declarations were representations that not only its accounts but also the
accounts of all of the plaintiffs, as trades accounts "for which the Owner
might anyway be held responsible", had been paid in full.  The plaintiffs
say that as the construction project manager, Colter only made the declarations
regarding its own accounts, and had no responsibility to ensure payment of the trades,
whose accounts were paid directly by Squamish JV or VW Hotels.

[
72
]

By its proposed counterclaim, Servus claims that
but for receipt of the draw request documents, including Colter's declarations
confirming that payments were made as declared, Servus would not have continued
to make the loan advances.  Servus pleads that no later than June 2009, Squamish
JV fell into default of its payment obligations to Colter and the trades, resulting
in the trades abandoning the worksite.  Servus alleges that Colter made
statutory declarations knowing they were false and that Servus reasonably
relied upon those false statements in continuing to advance funds under the
mortgage loan.  Servus claims that as a result of Colter's false
representations, it suffered damages of at least $704,000.

[
73
]

The critical piece of evidence that Servus
relies upon in support of its counterclaim is an email dated October 26, 2009
from Mr. Terry Leroux, a vice-president of Colter, to Mr. Babcock.  Mr. Leroux
said this:

Essentially
June, July and August there was very little work done... . We even put Squamish
JV and Ventures West on notice for termination of contract to try to get
payments caught up... . The trades are slowly and cautiously returning to the
site as some payments have been made... .  We have been supplying materials,
labour and rentals at cost.  Then we have to wait for months to get paid.  As
of this Friday Oct 30 Squamish JV will owe us $257,000 in due and overdue
payments.  I am not going to finance you anymore.  All we are asking is you
make the payments on their due date as per the contract, no more, no less.

[
74
]

That email is Exhibit A to affidavit no. 1 of Mr. Babcock
filed January 26, 2015.

[
75
]

On October 19, 2009 Colter delivered a statutory
declaration to Servus confirming that the last application for progress payment
for which it had received payment was dated August 31, 2009.  By a further
statutory declaration dated November 2, 2009 Colter certified that the last
payment for which it had received payment was for the progress draw dated
September 30, 2009.

[
76
]

Servus says that based on these statutory
declarations the payments appeared to be up-to-date in October and November
2009 and that it relied upon Colter's statutory declarations in continuing to
advance funds.

The test for extending time

[
77
]

The court's discretion to extend any period of
time provided in the
Rules
is set out in Rule 22-4(2):

Extending or shortening time

(2)        The
court may extend or shorten any period of time provided for in these Supreme
Court Civil Rules or in an order of the court, even though the application for
the extension or the order granting the extension is made after the period of
time has expired.

[
78
]

The court may extend the time for filing a
counterclaim where it is just and convenient to do so, having regard to the
following factors, first stated by Saunders J., as she then was, in
Squamish
Indian Band v. Canadian Pacific Ltd.
,
1998 CanLII 3909 (BC SC)
, [1998] B.C.J. No. 1726 (S.C.)
and more recently summarized by Madam Justice Gray in
Smith v. British
Columbia
,
2010 BCSC 928
at para.
19
:

In
Squamish Indian Band v. Canadian
Pacific Ltd.
,
1998 CanLII 3909 (BC SC)
, [1998] B.C.J. No. 1726 (S.C.), Saunders J. (when she was
a member of this Court), held that the following factors should be considered
in making any determination of whether it is just and convenient to extend the
time to permit a counterclaim to be filed:

a)         What
was the length of the delay between receiving the statement of claim and
proposing the draft counterclaim;

b)         What
were the reasons for delay;

c)         Whether
the counterclaim would be time barred but for
s. 4(1)
of the
Limitation
Act
;

d)         The
connection between the proposed counterclaim and the plaintiff's claim;

e)         Whether
there will be prejudice to the defendant, such as would arise if denial of the
application to file a counterclaim would prevent the defendant from making full
answer and defence to the claim brought against it; and

f)          Whether there
will be prejudice to the plaintiff by permitting the proposed counterclaim,
such as if the counterclaim would require additional investigation and
potentially delay the trial of the matter.

[
79
]

For the following reasons I am satisfied that on
the application of these factors to the particular circumstances of this
action, it is just and convenient to extend the time for Servus to file its
counterclaim.

Length of delay

[
80
]

Servus was served with the amended notice of
civil claim, by which it was added as a defendant, on or about May 1, 2012.
The notice of application attaching the proposed counterclaim was filed on
February 12, 2015, approximately two years and 10 months after the amended
notice of civil claim.

[
81
]

Although there has been delay on the part of Servus
in bringing its proposed counterclaim, the plaintiffs have not prosecuted this
action with any dispatch until recently.  On October 19, 2012, some months
after the plaintiffs added Servus and Mr. Babcock as defendants, they
applied for an order to renew their amended notice of civil claim and for an
order for alternative service on the defendant Brian Ostrander.  Material filed
in support of that application showed that the plaintiffs' last attempt to
serve Mr. Ostrander had been on May 29, 2012, but through oversight the notice
of civil claim had expired.  On November 2, 2012 the court granted the order to
renew the amended notice of civil claim.  Lists of documents were not exchanged
until April 2013.  On August 27, 2014 the plaintiffs conducted their first
examination for discovery, when they examined Mr. Babcock.  On January 26
and February 11, 2015 respectively, Mr. Babcock and Servus filed
applications for the dismissal by summary trial of the plaintiffs' action as against
them.  Those applications are presently set for hearing on April 10, 2015.  The
plaintiffs have scheduled an examination for discovery of a representative of Servus
for April 1, 2015.  The plaintiffs have not, as yet, set this action down for
trial.  On the hearing of this application, counsel advised that the next
available dates for a 10-day trial were in September 2016.

Reasons for delay

[
82
]

Servus maintains that it only discovered that
Colter knew that Squamish JV had failed to pay its accounts while Servus was
making loan advances as a result of the delivery on January 26, 2015 of Mr. Babcock's
affidavit, which attached Mr. Leroux's email of October 26, 2009 as an
exhibit.

[
83
]

The plaintiffs say that Servus ought to have
known much earlier that Colter and the other trades had not been paid on time
for their work.  First, the plaintiffs say that Servus' quantity surveyor
attended the site and would have observed that construction had halted when the
trades withdrew.  Second, the plaintiffs point out that Mr. Leroux's
October 26, 2009 email was listed in their list of documents, and in the list
of documents of Mr. Babcock, delivered in April and May 2013 respectively.

[
84
]

Counsel for the plaintiffs has not referred the
court to any report of the quantity surveyor that disclosed that the trades had
withdrawn from the Holiday Inn project, or that referred to any work for which
the plaintiffs had not been paid.

[
85
]

However, by May 2013, following delivery of the
lists of documents of the plaintiffs and Mr. Babcock, Servus had
sufficient information to investigate and determine whether it had a cause of
action against Colter.  Servus apparently failed to make that determination
until late January 2015.  Accordingly, I conclude that Servus is responsible
for the delay after May 2013 in bringing the counterclaim.  That is a factor
which weighs against the extension of time for filing the counterclaim.

Whether the counterclaim would be barred by the
Limitation Act

[
86
]

Counsel for the plaintiffs and Servus agree that
the counterclaim is not time barred.  If the date by which Servus knew or
reasonably ought to have known of its cause of action against Colter was May
2013, (or even June 2009, when payments were missed), then, by
s. 30
of the
Limitation
Act
, S.B.C. 2012, c. 13, which came into force on June 1, 2013, the former
Limitation
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266, applies.  Under s. 3(6) of that Act, the limitation
period would be six years, and has not expired.  Conversely, if,  contrary to
my earlier finding regarding the information available to it by May 2013, Servus
only had sufficient knowledge of a cause of action against Colter in January
2015, its counterclaim falls within the two-year limitation period under the current

Limitation Act
.  The absence of any limitations issue is a consideration
favouring the applicant.

The connection between the proposed counterclaim and the plaintiffs'
claim

[
87
]

There is a clear connection between the claim of
the plaintiffs and the proposed counterclaim.  In both its defence to the
plaintiffs' claim and its counterclaim, Servus raises its reliance on the draw
request documents, and particularly, the statutory declarations completed by
Colter.  While Servus counterclaims against only one plaintiff, the trial of
both the action and the counterclaim will require an examination of the same
facts relating to Colter's knowledge and obligations in completing the
statutory declarations, and the respective roles of Colter and Servus in the Holiday
Inn project, as well as the events leading to the failure of that project.

[
88
]

If the court denied this application, it would
be open to Servus to commence a separate action and then apply to have it tried
with this action.  If the court permits the filing of the counterclaim, the
parties would be spared unnecessary costs and a multiplicity of proceedings.

[
89
]

The plaintiffs say there is a substantial
difference between the relief they seek and the relief sought by the counterclaim.
The plaintiffs allege breach of trust and seek a declaration that the advances
made by Servus were impressed with a trust in favour of the plaintiffs
collectively.  Servus has limited its counterclaim to one plaintiff and claims
damages for negligent or fraudulent misrepresentation.  Again, despite the
differences in the specific remedies sought, all of the relief claimed by the
parties relates to the role of Servus as the lender for the Holiday Inn project,
and the respective rights, duties and obligations of the parties under the draw
request system in place for the project.

Prejudice to defendant if the application were denied

[
90
]

Servus would not be prevented from pursuing the
same relief in a separate action if its application for leave to file the
counterclaim were denied.  However, given the close connection between the
plaintiffs' claims and the counterclaim, all matters should be dealt with in
the same action.  Servus would be put to additional and unnecessary costs if it
were required to defend this action and bring a separate proceeding in which
much of the same evidence would be adduced.

[
91
]

If Servus were to succeed in establishing the
facts pleaded in support of the counterclaim, it would have a full answer and
defence to the plaintiffs' claims.  I am satisfied Servus may suffer some
prejudice in making a full answer and defence if it is denied leave to bring
its counterclaim in this action.

Prejudice to the plaintiff by permitting the proposed counterclaim

[
92
]

Colter says it will be prejudiced if it is now
required to defend against allegations of fraudulent and negligent
representation which were raised for the first time more than five years after
the events giving rise to this action.  The plaintiff also says that its
witnesses' memories of the events surrounding the execution of the statutory
declarations have faded with the passage of time.  The plaintiffs say they will
all be prejudiced to the extent that adding the counterclaim against Colter
complicates the trial and delays a final resolution of this action.

[
93
]

If the counterclaim is permitted, Colter will
have to undertake some additional investigations.  That plaintiff will have to
search for and disclose any documents in its possession or control concerning
its knowledge of any delay in the payment by Squamish JV of its own accounts,
and its knowledge of whether or not the trades were being paid on time.  While
that investigation may put Colter to some additional time and expense, here, where
no trial date has been set, it will not delay final resolution of this matter.

[
94
]

There is potential for prejudice to Colter from
the passage of time.  However, the passing of time since the events giving rise
to this action, and its effects on witnesses' memories is a factor that already
affects all of the parties.  For example, the passage of time may well affect
witnesses' recollection of the events relating to the October 26, 2009 meeting
when Mr. Babcock is alleged to have promised to pay the trades
personally.  In my view, the passage of time is a neutral factor in this case.

[
95
]

The plaintiffs have not yet conducted
discoveries of Servus; the plaintiffs' representatives have not been examined
for discovery; and no trial date has been set.  In these circumstances,
permitting the counterclaim is unlikely to delay the resolution of the
plaintiffs' claims.  In light of the close connection between the action and
the counterclaim, allowing Servus to bring the counterclaim is also unlikely to
substantially extend the time required for trial or to significantly complicate
the issues for determination by the court.

[
96
]

Having weighed all of these factors, I grant Servus
leave to file a counterclaim, substantially in the form attached as Schedule A
to its notice of application, and have concluded that it is just and convenient
to extend the time for filing the counterclaim to March 25, 2015.

Security for Costs

[
97
]

Section 236
of the
BCA
sets out the
statutory basis for an order for security for costs against a corporation:

If a corporation
is the plaintiff in a legal proceeding brought before the court, and if it
appears that the corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant
if the defendant is successful in the defence, the court may require security
to be given by the corporation for those costs, and may stay all legal
proceedings until the security is given.

[
98
]

The applicant must establish a
prima facie

case that the plaintiff company would be unable to pay the applicant's cost if
the plaintiff's claim fails.  If the applicant meets that burden, then the
plaintiff company may resist an order for security for costs by showing it has
sufficient exigible assets to satisfy an award of costs, or that there is no
arguable defence to the claim:
Devocht v. Hallgren
,
2015 BCSC 149

citing
Integrated Contractors Ltd. v. Leduc Development Ltd.
,
2009 BCSC
965
and
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.).

[
99
]

Once the applicant has shown that the plaintiff
company will not be able to pay costs should its claim fail, the court will
generally order security for costs, unless there is no arguable defence:
Fat
Mel's Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Company
(1993),

1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (2d) 231 (C.A.) at para.
16
.

[
100
]

In
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd.
(1997),
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29 B.C.L.R.
(3d) 252 (C.A.), Finch J.A. (as he then was) described the principles stated by
the English Court of Appeal in
Keary Development v. Tarmac Construction
,

[1995] 3 All. E.R. 534
as a useful guide to the court's exercise of discretion
on an application for security for costs:

1.

The court has a complete discretion whether to
order security, and will act in light of all the relevant circumstances;

2.

The possibility or probability that the
plaintiff company will be deterred from pursuing its claim is not without more
sufficient reason for not ordering security;

3.

The court must attempt to balance injustices
arising from use of security as an instrument of oppression to stifle a
legitimate claim on the one hand, and use of impecuniosity as a means of
putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the other;

4.

The court may have regard to the merits of the
action, but should avoid going into detail on the merits unless success or
failure appears obvious;

5.

The court can order any amount of security up to
the full amount claimed, as long as the amount is more than nominal;

6.

Before the court refuses to order security on
the ground that it would unfairly stifle a valid claim, the court must be
satisfied that, in all the circumstances, it is probable that the claim would
be stifled; and

7.

The lateness of the application for security is
a circumstance which can properly be taken into account.

[
101
]

The plaintiffs bear the onus of proving the absence of an arguable
defence:
Devocht
at para.
67
.

[
102
]

Each of the plaintiffs is a company that was incorporated under the
BCA
.

[
103
]

Registry searches conducted by Servus show that Colter is a company
in good standing. However, Colter holds no real property in the province of
British Columbia and has registered security interests charging all of its
present and after-acquired property in favour of the Royal Bank of Canada.

[
104
]

The plaintiff Granite Art Masonry Ltd. was dissolved on September
10, 2012 for failure to file records with the registrar of companies, and owns
no real property in the province.

[
105
]

The plaintiff Pipeline is in receivership.  Its claim has been assigned
to Colter and Mustang.  Pipeline owns no real property and has registered
security interests charging all of its present and after-acquired property.

[
106
]

While the plaintiffs Fisher Painting Ltd. and C & E
Building Products Inc. are both in good standing, neither owns real property in
British Columbia and both have registered security interests against all of
their present and after-acquired property.

[
107
]

Finally, Mustang is a company in good standing but holds no
registered interest in real property in the province, other than a claim of
builders lien valued at $12,136.43.  All of Mustang's present and
after-acquired property is charged by registered security interests in favour
of Coast Capital Savings Credit Union.

[
108
]

I find that Servus has made out a
prima facie
case that none
of the plaintiffs will be able to pay its costs if the plaintiffs' claim fails.

[
109
]

The only two plaintiffs who have tendered evidence on this
application are Colter and Mustang, whose claims against the defendants
represent 85 per cent of the plaintiffs' total claim of $1,237,384.48.

[
110
]

Neither Colter nor Mustang has alleged that posting security would
stifle their ability to pursue this litigation.  Rather, Colter and Mustang
have attempted to show that they do have sufficient exigible assets to satisfy
any costs award.  Mr. Kelly Leroux has sworn that although the company
suffered significant losses as a result of the Holiday Inn project, Colter has
been able to continue its business and make profits.  Mr. Leroux has
deposed that he has reviewed Colter's unaudited accounting information for
2014, that Colter's general revenue for 2014 exceeded $2.8 million and that the
company's estimated net income for 2014 is around $250,000.

[
111
]

Mr. Doug Johnston, the principal of Mustang, has sworn that
Mustang is a business that has been in operation for about 20 years, and that
although his company suffered significant losses as a result of the Holiday Inn
project, Mustang has also been able to continue its business and make profits.
Based on advice from the corporate bookkeeper, Mr. Johnston has sworn that
Mustang's estimated general revenue for 2014 was $1.6 million and that its
estimated net income for 2014 exceeds $30,000.  He has also deposed that to his
knowledge Mustang's creditors are satisfied with the company's loan
arrangements and payments, and that Mustang currently has no significant debts
outstanding.

[
112
]

Neither Mr. Leroux for Colter, nor Mr. Johnston for Mustang
has attached to their affidavit any financial statements, balance sheets,
statements of income and expense, or lists of accounts receivable or payable.
Neither plaintiff has adduced any evidence of the value of any current
contracts.  As Servus submits, the fact that Colter and Mustang may each have
earned net income in 2014 does not establish that either company continues to
hold those amounts in cash or as an otherwise exigible asset.

[
113
]

I find that the evidence of the plaintiffs falls short of
establishing that they will have exigible assets to pay the defendant's cost if
their claims against Servus fail.

[
114
]

I turn now to the question of whether the plaintiffs have met their
onus of satisfying the court there is no arguable defence to their claim.

[
115
]

The plaintiffs' claim against Servus for breach of trust and for the
tort of knowingly assisting Squamish JV's wrongful diversion of funds advanced
by Servus for the Holiday Inn project.

[
116
]

Mr. Leroux and Mr. Johnston have each sworn that they are
not aware of any facts that could reasonably give rise to a defence to the
plaintiffs' claim against Servus.  While I have considered that evidence, there
are other factors which I must also take into consideration.  The plaintiffs
claim equitable relief against Servus, a commercial lender to Squamish JV, in
the form of a declaration that the funds advanced to Squamish JV were subject
to a constructive trust in their favour.

[
117
]

Servus argues that a compelling juristic reason exists for the
denial of equitable relief to the plaintiffs.  The defendant says that it is
contrary to the reasonable expectations of the parties and public policy
considerations that a commercial lender who has advanced funds to a borrower in
accordance with the credit facilities in place could also be a constructive
trustee of those funds for parties with whom it has no direct or contractual
relationship.  Servus contends that the doctrine of constructive trust may not
be invoked to circumvent statutory priorities.  In support of its position, Servus
refers to
Caterpillar Financial Services v. 360networks corporation et al
,

2007 BCCA 14
,
Pacific Shores Resort & Spa Ltd. (Re)
,
2013 BCSC 480

and
Sabihi v. Dr. Mansur Roy Inc.
,
2013 BCSC 1571
.

[
118
]

In
Caterpillar Financial Services
, the appellant sought to
recover amounts owing under equipment leases where it had failed to file
financing statements under the
Personal Property Security Act
, R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 359.  Caterpillar claimed that the proceeds of sale of the leased
equipment were impressed with a constructive trust in its favour, based on
unjust enrichment.  The Court of Appeal held that Caterpillar "appears to
be employing the remedy of a constructive trust to vault its security position
in respect of [the equipment] contrary to the provisions of the
PPSA
and
the general framework of the
CCAA
", and upheld the trial judge's
finding that Caterpillar's failure to perfect its security interest constituted
a juristic reason for denying recovery:
Caterpillar

Financial
Services
at paras.
64 and 65
.

[
119
]

In
Pacific Shores Resort & Spa Ltd. (Re)
, Madam Justice
Fitzpatrick observed at para. 32 that the application of equitable principles
in the context of a statutory priority regime "inevitably gives rise to
the suggestion that the fundamental purpose of the legislation would be
undermined if equity is wielded to defeat statutory priorities."

[
120
]

Servus also relies upon
Sabihi
, at para.
48
, for the
proposition that courts rarely apply equitable remedies, such as unjust
enrichment, in the commercial construction context, and that except in unusual
circumstances a subcontractor's remedies are limited to its claims in contract
and its remedies against the property under the
Builders Lien Act
,
S.B.C. 1997, c. 45.

[
121
]

Here, Servus argues that it reasonably relied upon the draw request
documents prepared by Squamish JV and Colter in advancing funds for the Holiday
Inn project.  Further, Servus argues that it holds a properly and validly
perfected security interest ranking in priority to the claims of the
plaintiffs, who failed to register their claims of builders lien until after Servus
had advanced the full amount of the mortgage loan to Squamish JV.  Servus
contends that in these circumstances, both the reasonable expectations of the
parties and public policy considerations provide a juristic reason for denying
the plaintiffs' recovery on their claims in trust.

[
122
]

With respect to their claim for knowing assistance, the plaintiffs
must prove that:

(a)       the funds advanced by Servus were impressed with a trust
in their favour;

(b)       Servus had knowledge of the trust and the fraudulent and
dishonest conduct of Squamish JV and/or Mr. Ostrander giving rise to the
breach; and

(c)        Servus either participated or assisted in the fraudulent
and dishonest conduct.

PricewaterhouseCoopers
Inc. v. Flash & The Boys, LLC
,
2014 BCSC 1093

at para.
11
.

[
123
]

Again, Servus submits that it was entitled to rely, and did rely
upon the draw request documents before advancing funds and says that it only
acquired knowledge of any possible wrongdoing by Squamish JV or Mr. Ostrander
through a report issued by the receiver MNP long after the funds were advanced.

[
124
]

It will be for the trial judge to determine the merits of this
action.  However, on this application, I find that Servus has arguable defences
to the plaintiffs' claims.

[
125
]

I have found that the defendant has established a
prima facie

case that the plaintiffs are without exigible assets and that the plaintiffs
have not shown they would be able to pay the defendant's costs, or that the
defendants have no arguable case.  I am persuaded that this is an appropriate
case for an order for security for costs.

[
126
]

The defendant seeks security for costs in the amount of $47,460,
based upon its estimate of the party-and-party costs for a 10-day trial of the
plaintiffs' action.   Part of that time may be devoted to the hearing of the
defendant's counterclaim.  Bearing in mind my discretion to order security in
any amount up to the full amount claimed, I order that the plaintiffs post
security for the costs of Servus in the amount of $40,000 within 30 days of the
date of this order.

[
127
]

The action is stayed until such time as the plaintiffs post security
for costs in the amount of $40,000.

[
128
]

In the event the plaintiffs fail to post the security ordered within
30 days of the date of this order, the plaintiffs' action as against Servus
will be dismissed as abandoned, without further order of the court and without
prejudice to the defendant's counterclaim.

Costs

[
129
]

The defendant Babcock was successful in resisting the plaintiffs’
application to add the claim of unjust enrichment and will have the costs of
that application, at Scale B, in any event of the cause.

[
130
]

The defendant Servus will also have the costs of
each of its applications at Scale B.

“PEARLMAN
J.”
